author: A Robot
objectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
Compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Students observe Mars from a simulated Earth-based night-sky perspective, watching it drift eastward against the stars, slow down, loop westward in retrograde, and then resume its eastward drift.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Recognize that retrograde motion is a temporary, periodic phenomenon occurring roughly every 26 months.
instructions: Face the star field and watch Mars's position relative to the background constellations over the simulated weeks.
Use the Next button to advance through each stage of Mars's apparent path.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial staging of the Earth-sky scene: star field and Mars appear at their starting position with introductory labels visible.
clips.narration: Here we see the night sky as viewed from Earth's surface, with Mars positioned among the background stars. Over the coming weeks, watch closely how Mars's position shifts relative to the fixed constellations behind it.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves rightward (eastward) across the star field to depict its normal prograde drift, and the date label updates to show time passing.
clips.narration: Normally, Mars drifts slowly eastward against the background stars, night after night, week after week.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars's position shifts slightly westward and upward to begin tracing the retrograde loop shape, illustrating the slowdown and reversal.
clips.narration: But roughly every 26 months, something strange happens: Mars slows down, stops its eastward march, and begins to loop backward toward the west.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars continues moving further westward and dips downward, completing the visible arc of the retrograde loop.
clips.narration: For about two months, Mars continues its westward loop, tracing a small backward arc against the stars before slowing again.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves back toward the east, completing the loop shape and returning to prograde motion; date label reflects the passage of additional weeks.
clips.narration: Finally, Mars resumes its normal eastward drift, completing the retrograde loop and continuing its long-term eastward journey across the constellations.

modules.description: Students compare the awkward geocentric epicycle explanation of Mars's loop with the elegant heliocentric explanation, setting up the outside-solar-system view in the next scene.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
instructions: Compare the two orbital models side by side.
Notice how the geocentric model requires an extra small loop (epicycle) to explain Mars's path, while the heliocentric model needs no such addition.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the geocentric diagram with an orbiting epicycle marker to show how ancient astronomers artificially generated the loop shape.
clips.narration: To explain Mars's backward loop, the ancient geocentric model, with Earth at the center, required Mars to move along a small circle called an epicycle, layered on top of its main orbit. This produced the loop, but only through an awkward, ad hoc addition.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the heliocentric diagram to emphasize its simplicity in contrast to the geocentric epicycle, updating the comparison label.
clips.narration: The heliocentric model, with the Sun at the center, explains the very same loop with no extra machinery at all. It simply falls out of the geometry of Earth and Mars moving on their own separate orbits around the Sun.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Outside View of Earth and Mars Orbits
modules.description: Students view the solar system from outside, watching Earth and Mars move on their heliocentric orbits, and see how Earth overtaking Mars produces the apparent retrograde loop, analogous to passing a slower car.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
instructions: Watch the Sun, Earth, and Mars from a top-down viewpoint outside the solar system.
Observe the line of sight from Earth to Mars as both planets orbit, and see how the projected position of Mars against the distant stars traces the retrograde loop.

components.text: View from Outside the Solar System

clips.changeMeaning: Establishes the outside solar-system viewpoint with the Sun, Earth, and Mars visible on their respective orbits, orbit animations begin.
clips.narration: Now let's step outside the solar system entirely. Here we see the Sun at the center, with Earth on its faster, inner orbit and Mars on its slower, outer orbit.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces a visible sight line from Earth to Mars to help students track the changing direction of the line of sight as Earth catches up to Mars.
clips.narration: Earth moves faster because it is closer to the Sun. As Earth approaches and then passes Mars on the inside track, watch the sight line connecting Earth to Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: No new objects are added; this clip lets the orbit animation continue playing while the narration draws the highway-passing analogy over the moving sight line.
clips.narration: This is just like passing a slower car on the highway: as you overtake it, it briefly appears to drift backward relative to the distant scenery, even though it never actually reverses direction.

components.text: This Sweep Creates the Retrograde Loop

clips.changeMeaning: Concludes the outside view by tying the sight-line sweep directly to the retrograde loop observed earlier from Earth's surface, reinforcing the causal link.
clips.narration: As the sight line sweeps backward and then forward again, this is exactly what produces Mars's apparent retrograde loop against the background stars, with no epicycles required.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
modules.description: Students compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn from the outside solar-system view, observing that more distant planets produce smaller, less dramatic loops.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.
instructions: Observe the three outer planets on their orbits alongside Earth.
Compare the size of each planet's projected retrograde loop as displayed above it.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces Jupiter and Saturn into the outside-view scene alongside Earth and Mars, all with orbit animations enabled for comparison.
clips.narration: Let's add Jupiter and Saturn to our outside view, alongside Earth and Mars, all orbiting the Sun at their own distances and speeds.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights Mars specifically to draw attention to its comparatively large loop size, updating the label to focus on Mars.
clips.narration: Mars, being closest to Earth's orbit among the three, shows the largest and most dramatic retrograde loop, since the relative motion between Earth and Mars is most pronounced.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts focus to Jupiter, updating the label to describe its smaller loop relative to Mars.
clips.narration: Jupiter, much farther away, moves far more slowly along its orbit. Earth still overtakes it, but the resulting loop is smaller and less pronounced against the stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts focus to Saturn, updating the label to complete the comparison and reinforce the pattern of decreasing loop size with distance.
clips.narration: Saturn, farther still and slower yet, produces the smallest and most subtle retrograde loop of the three, though the same basic overtaking effect is still at work.
